'''Howard Brenner''' (16 March 1929 – 17 February 2014) was a professor emeritus of chemical engineering at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. His research profoundly influenced the field of [[fluid dynamics]], and his research contribution to fundamental principles of fluid dynamics has been deeply honored.<ref name="AICHE">{{cite web|title=Memorial Session in Honor of Howard Brenner (Invited Talks)|url=https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2014/webprogram/Session28260.html|website=AICHE|publisher=}}</ref>
His first textbook, Low Reynolds Number Hydrodynamics (with Happel; Prentice-Hall, 1965), earned him a reputation lasting several decades.<ref name=book>{{cite book|last1=Happel|first1=John|last2=Brenner|first2=Howard|title=Low Reynolds Number Hydrodynamics |publisher=Martinus Nijhoff Publishers|series= Mechanics of Fluids and Transport Processes |volume=1|date=1983|doi=10.1007/978-94-009-8352-6 |isbn=978-94-009-8352-6}}</ref>
His profession though fundamental research is on microfluidics, complex liquids, interfacial transport process, emulsion rheology, and multiphase flows.<ref name="Faculty news">{{cite web|title=Howard Brenner, professor emeritus of chemical engineering, passes away at 84|url=https://news.mit.edu/2014/howard-brenner-professor-emeritus-of-chemical-engineering-passes-away-at-84|website=MIT news|date=25 February 2014 |publisher=MIT PRESS|access-date=February 25, 2014}}</ref><ref name="Faculty ChemE news">{{cite web|title=Howard Brenner, professor emeritus of chemical engineering|url=http://web.mit.edu/cheme/news/2014/hbrenner.html|website=MIT ChemE news|publisher=MIT PRESS}}</ref>

==Career==
Brenner earned his bachelor's degree from [[Pratt Institute]] (1950), and his master's (1954) and DEngSc (1957) from [[New York University]], both in chemical engineering. He has served on the chemical engineering faculties of New York University (1955–1966), [[Carnegie Mellon University]] (1966–1977), [[University of Rochester]] (1977–1981, department chair), and MIT (1981–2005). Since 1981, he was a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (William Henry Dow Professor). He was a visiting professor at the [[University of Minnesota]], [[Caltech]] (Fairchild Scholar 1975/76, Chevron Visiting Professor 1988/89), and [[Technion]] (Visiting Professor of Mechanical Engineering 1996).

==Honors and awards==
He received the 2001 Fluid Dynamics Prize from the Division of Fluid Dynamics of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref name="Fluid Dynamics Prize-APS">{{cite web|title=Howard Brenner, 2001 Fluid Dynamics Prize Recipient|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?first_nm=Howard&last_nm=Brenner&year=2001|website=APS Physics|publisher=}}</ref> the 1980 [[Bingham Medal]] of the [[Society of Rheology]] and the Warren K. Lewis Award (1999) from the [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers]]. He was a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (1980)<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Professor Howard Brenner
 |url=https://www.nae.edu/29651/Professor-Howard-Brenner
 |website=National Academy of Engineering
 |access-date=11 April 2026
}}</ref> and [[National Academy of Sciences]] (2000).<ref name="NAE">{{cite web|title=Howard Brenner, National Academy of Sciences |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/howard-brenner-bhn2jz/|website=NAS|publisher=}}</ref> He was elected as the fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (1999),<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Howard Brenner
 |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/howard-brenner
 |website=American Academy of Arts &amp; Sciences
 |access-date=11 April 2026
}}</ref> the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and the [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers]].
